items.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.tldr: President Donald Trump claimed the FBI is probing an alleged affair between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a woman identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The episode has rattled Nvidia's market value, raised U.S. security concerns over AI chip exports, and sparked a political flashpoint between Washington and Beijing.
items.background: Nvidia, the world’s second‑largest public company after Apple, designs the GPUs that power today’s generative‑AI boom. Its flagship H200 and Blackwell chips are deemed dual‑use technologies, capable of accelerating both civilian AI workloads and military‑grade simulations. In recent months the U.S. government has tightened export licences for Nvidia’s most advanced products, citing national‑security risks. Against that backdrop, reports emerged that Jensen Huang had a personal relationship with Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), a Singapore‑based executive of Megaspeed who is alleged by U.S. intelligence to be a Beijing spy. The story gained political traction when former President Donald Trump publicly asked Huang whether he knew his partner was a spy, and said the FBI was investigating the matter. The Chinese foreign ministry dismissed the allegations as “groundless”.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical Stakes
analysis.content: The episode sits at the intersection of three strategic currents: U.S. attempts to contain China’s AI ascendancy, Beijing’s alleged use of personal relationships for intelligence gathering, and the politicisation of technology security in Washington. If the FBI uncovers substantive evidence that Alice Huang sought to funnel Nvidia’s cutting‑edge chips to the People’s Republic of China, it would provide a concrete illustration of the espionage risk that U.S. officials have warned about for years. Conversely, a lack of hard proof could reinforce Beijing’s narrative that the United States is weaponising export controls to stifle competition. The episode also feeds into a broader narrative championed by Trump and other hawks that China’s AI progress threatens to “super‑charge” its surveillance state and military capabilities.

analysis.heading: Corporate Governance and Legal Risks
analysis.content: Nvidia’s board has commissioned an independent review of the alleged affair, but the company has publicly stated it sees no indication that trade secrets were compromised. Nevertheless, the market reaction—more than $250 billion erased from Nvidia’s market cap and a 4 % share‑price drop—highlights investor sensitivity to governance scandals involving high‑tech firms. A parallel class‑action lawsuit in California alleges that Nvidia concealed the relationship from shareholders, potentially exposing the firm to billions in damages if the case proceeds. The situation underscores the need for tighter internal controls over personal relationships that intersect with national‑security‑sensitive business units, especially in firms that sit at the core of the AI supply chain.

analysis.heading: AI Technology and Export Controls
analysis.content: Nvidia’s H200 and Blackwell chips are subject to the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Entity List and the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). In January 2024 the Trump administration granted conditional licences for the H200 to select Chinese customers, but the most advanced Blackwell family remains blocked. Any proven attempt to smuggle these chips would likely trigger a reassessment of the licensing framework, potentially tightening restrictions across the entire semiconductor sector. Moreover, the case may accelerate bipartisan legislative pushes for a “National AI Security Act” that would codify mandatory security vetting for AI‑critical hardware manufacturers.

analysis.heading: US Domestic Political Dynamics
analysis.content: Trump’s public comments serve multiple political purposes. By positioning himself as a defender of American security, he attempts to reclaim the narrative on China from the Biden administration and appeal to his base’s anti‑China sentiment. At the same time, the remarks place pressure on congressional committees that are slated to hold a closed‑door briefing with Jensen Huang, forcing lawmakers to confront the issue publicly. The episode also revives the long‑standing debate over the role of former presidents in influencing ongoing investigations, raising questions about the separation of powers and the independence of the FBI.

key_facts: Nvidia’s market value fell by roughly $250 billion after the affair was disclosed
President Trump said he asked Jensen Huang whether he knew his partner was a spy and claimed the FBI is investigating
Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, is alleged by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese intelligence asset
Nvidia has launched an independent internal investigation and faces a class‑action lawsuit in California
China’s foreign ministry called the allegations “entirely groundless”
implications: Potential tightening of U.S. export controls on AI‑critical chips if espionage is confirmed
Increased scrutiny of corporate governance practices at high‑tech firms with national‑security relevance
Possible escalation of U.S.–China diplomatic tensions over technology security
Shareholder activism and litigation risk for Nvidia and similar AI‑chip makers
Political capital for Trump and other hard‑liners in the U.S. Congress
items.outlook: In the short term, Nvidia will likely cooperate with the FBI and congressional inquiries while attempting to stabilise its stock price through transparent communication. If the investigation uncovers concrete espionage activity, Washington may impose stricter export bans on Nvidia’s most advanced GPUs, prompting the company to diversify its supply chain and possibly relocate portions of its R&D. Conversely, a clean‑bill outcome could bolster Nvidia’s reputation for resilience and may be used by the administration to argue that existing export controls are sufficient. The broader U.S.–China AI rivalry will continue to intensify, with this episode serving as a cautionary tale for other semiconductor firms operating in the gray zone between commercial competition and national security.

items.fulltext:
Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (Â£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.
Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
- What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
  - Published3 hours ago
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.
The American firm, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating Nvidia's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.
Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
'He said he had no idea she was a spy'
At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.
He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".
Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.
The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.
Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.
A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".
Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.
- Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
  - Published5 hours ago
- AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values 
  - Published3 days ago
Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.
Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.
It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.
Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

items.title: Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
items.tldr: The UK government is expected to water down its electric vehicle (EV) targets, moving from 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030 to a lower threshold, a move welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups ahead of COP31.
items.background: Under current rules, 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030, with all new cars required to be zero-emission by 2035. The government has been consulting on reducing its 80% rule, and a significant reduction is now expected. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has recused himself from the issue due to his wife's links to an electric vehicle company. Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh will lead the consultations. Industry groups including Energy UK and the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) have opposed the move, warning that weakened targets could damage investment certainty. The government maintains its commitment to net zero targets and its participation in COP31 in Turkey.

analysis.heading: Policy Impact and Climate Leadership
analysis.content: The proposed reduction of EV targets could undermine the UK's climate leadership position ahead of COP31 in Turkey. The 2030 and 2035 deadlines are central to the country's net zero strategy and its ability to attract green investment. A weaker target may signal regulatory uncertainty and could affect the UK's standing as a climate leader during the high-profile UN climate summit. This move comes amid ongoing debates about the pace of the transition to electric vehicles, with pressure from both industry groups and environmental organizations.

analysis.heading: Industry Response and Economic Considerations
analysis.content: The automotive industry, including Energy UK and the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), has welcomed the review of EV targets but warned that weakened targets could damage the investment certainty needed for infrastructure, innovation, and services required for the transition. Car manufacturers have long called for urgent relief from the current targets, arguing that the speed of the transition is too slow. The government's Zero Emission Vehicles (ZEV) mandate (28% by 2025, 33% by 2026, 80% by 2030) represents a gradual increase, but the proposed reduction would accelerate this timeline and potentially create market disruption for manufacturers and dealers.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical Context and EU Comparison
analysis.content: The European Union scrapped a similar plan to end new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035, creating a regional comparison with UK policy. While the UK government insists the reduction is driven by economic considerations rather than environmental priorities, the contrast with EU uncertainty highlights the UK's divergent approach to climate policy. This divergence could influence global perceptions of the UK's climate leadership and may affect international partnerships on green technology and infrastructure investment.

items.outlook: The government is expected to announce the specific changes in the coming weeks. The outcome will be closely watched by environmental groups, industry stakeholders, and international observers ahead of COP31. The decision could set a precedent for future policy adjustments on climate targets and influence the UK's broader climate policy trajectory.

items.fulltext:
Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
- Published
The UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced this week in a move likely to be welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups.
Under the current rules, 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 but industry groups have long called for "urgent relief".
New petrol or diesel cars are due to be phased out by 2030 and by 2035 all new cars must be zero emission.
But the speed of the transition to electric has been hotly debated, including within the cabinet.
The government has been consulting on reducing its 80% rule and a significant reduction is now expected.
Downing Street has insisted no decision has been made.
A government source told the BBC it would approach the issue in a "pragmatic and balanced" way.
If ministers do decide on a steeper watering-down of the rules, it will arguably be interpreted by some - alongside the approval of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea - as the government prioritising economic considerations over environmental ones.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has recused himself from this issue due to his wife's links to an electric vehicle company.
The key meetings on the subject will instead be chaired by Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh.
Asked about reports the targets would be reduced, Burnham dismissed this as "speculation", adding: "No decision has been made at this point."
Sustainability groups say any weakening of the 2030 target will threaten the UK's long-term electrification and climate goals.
It could undermine the UK's claim to be providing leadership on climate just as ministers head to Turkey for COP31, the UN's climate summit.
Energy UK, the trade association for the energy industry, has also opposed the move.
Last month, it said, external reducing targets could damage "the investment certainty needed to deliver the infrastructure, innovation and services required for the transition to zero-emission transport".
Asked if climate change was no longer a big priority, Health Minister Karin Smyth said the government was committed to its emissions targets.
"This country is doing great work in terms of our transition and looking at renewables â that's a key part of growth in different parts of the country," she told BBC Breakfast.
She added that the prime minister would have "a good story to tell" when meeting other leaders at COP31.
A government spokesperson said: "We are committed to the phase out of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets."
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders welcomed the government's review of the EV targets when it was announced in the summer.
Last week, head of the association Mike Hawes said transitioning to electric vehicles had come at a "heavy cost" with billions spent on discounts to drive demand in electric vehicles.
He said the government's targets could not be achieved "without putting at risk any future investment".
- UK electric car sales target set to be weakened 
  - Published14 June
- EU waters down plans to end new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035 
  - Published16 December 2025
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
The government's policy to phase out petrol and diesel vehicle sales has undergone multiple changes since it was first introduced by former Prime Minister Boris Johnson in 2020.
His successor Rishi Sunak pushed back the timeline to 2035, and the Burnham government set up a review of the EV sales targets in August.
Sunak introduced phased targets for EV sales in the UK, known as the Zero Emission Vehicles (ZEV) mandate.
Under the ZEV mandate, the percentage of new car sales that need to be EVs increases each year. The target was 28% for 2025, 33% for 2026, and so on until it reaches 80% by 2030.
Pressure in the European Union saw the bloc scrap a similar plan to ban new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035, particularly from countries with large auto industries such as Germany.
The Conservative Party has also vowed to abandon the petrol car ban if it wins the next election, with leader Kemi Badenoch calling it a "well-meaning, but ultimately destructive piece of legislation".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the government was "building up a shocking record of backsliding and bad decisions on climate issues".
